extracted.intended_audience: students and mathematicians (advanced undergraduate / graduate level readers and educators)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook material presenting definitions, theorems, lemmas, proofs, and worked examples in number theory and geometry (Riemann zeta function, polyhedra, decompositions, and basic graph incidence results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Riemann zeta function ζ(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: ζ(s) := Σ_{n≥1} 1/n^s for real s > 1, with a canonical continuation to the entire complex plane having a single simple pole at s = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Series converges for real s>1 (harmonic number estimate shows divergence at s=1). The analytic continuation (with pole at s=1) can be constructed using power series expansions. The zeta function is central to prime number theory; see Euler product and connections to zeros (Riemann hypothesis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler product formula for ζ(s)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due to Euler; encodes unique prime factorization. It follows from the geometric series expansion 1/(1 − p^{−s}) = 1 + p^{−s} + p^{−2s} + ... and multiplicativity over primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zagier's derivation of ζ(4) from ζ(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the function f(m,n) = 2/(m^3 n) + 1/(m^2 n^2) + 2/(m n^3) for m,n ≥ 1 and summing a telescoping/cancellation identity over m,n leads to 5 ζ(4) = 2 ζ(2)^2, hence ζ(4) = π^4/90 (with ζ(2)=π^2/6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof checks that f(m,n) − f(m+n,n) − f(m,m+n) = 2/(m^2 n^2), sums over m,n ≥ 1 so off-diagonal terms cancel, then equates sums to factor ζ(2)^2. Alternative derivations via Bernoulli numbers appear elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even zeta values are rational multiples of powers of π
rubrics_metrics.description: For even integer s ≥ 2, ζ(s) is a rational multiple of π^s, and therefore irrational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical results (Bernoulli number formulas) produce exact rational multiples. See Chapter 23 for Bernoulli-number derivations and references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known irrationality results for odd zeta values
rubrics_metrics.description: ζ(3) is irrational (Apéry, 1979); Ball & Rivoal proved infinitely many ζ(2t+1) are irrational; Zudilin proved at least one of ζ(5), ζ(7), ζ(9), ζ(11) is irrational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite progress, irrationality of specific odd zeta values ≥5 remains largely open. See Fischler survey and cited literature for further developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lagarias elementary equivalence to the Riemann hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to: for all n ≥ 1, Σ_{d|n} d ≤ H_n + exp(H_n) log(H_n), with equality only for n = 1 (H_n is the nth harmonic number).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This surprising equivalence translates the RH into an elementary inequality about divisors and harmonic numbers; reference: Lagarias (Amer. Math. Monthly 2002).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: equidecomposable polyhedra
rubrics_metrics.description: Two polyhedra P and Q are equidecomposable if they can be decomposed into finite sets of polyhedra P1,...,Pn and Q1,...,Qn such that Pi and Qi are congruent for all i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompositions may admit reflections or not; Gerling's theorem implies choice about reflections does not affect these definitions. This notion formalizes 'cut-and-reassemble' equivalence of solids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: equicomplementable polyhedra
rubrics_metrics.description: P and Q are equicomplementable if there exist polyhedra 'P and 'Q, obtained by adding finitely many congruent polyhedra to P and Q respectively, such that 'P and 'Q are equidecomposable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equidecomposability implies equicomplementability (take m = 0), but the converse is not automatic and is a central notion in Hilbert's third problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pearl Lemma (assignment-of-counts on segments)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P and Q are equidecomposable, then one can assign positive integers (pearls) to all segments of the decompositions P = ⋃ P_i and Q = ⋃ Q_i so that each edge of a piece P_k receives the same number of pearls as the corresponding edge of Q_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sets integer variables for segments and linear equations equating sums on corresponding edges. Existence of positive real solution (segment lengths) plus the Cone Lemma gives integer solutions. The lemma is used to compare angle sums across decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cone Lemma (integrality from positive real solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a system of homogeneous linear equations with integer coefficients has a positive real solution, then it also has a positive integer solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the solution set as a rational cone C = {x ∈ R^N: Ax = 0, x > 0}. By scaling and Fourier–Motzkin elimination one shows the lexicographically smallest solution with xi ≥ 1 is rational; multiplying by a common denominator yields an integer solution. Useful to convert real-valued combinatorial constraints (like segment lengths) into integer assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bricard's condition (angle-sum integrality condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If 3-dimensional polyhedra P and Q with dihedral angles α1,...,α_r and β1,...,β_s are equidecomposable (or more generally equicomplementable), then there exist positive integers m_i, n_j and an integer k such that m1 α1 + ... + m_r α_r = n1 β1 + ... + n_s β_s + k π.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: place pearls per the Pearl Lemma and sum dihedral angles at pearls to obtain integer-weighted sums Σ1 and Σ2 for P and Q; congruent corresponding pieces force Σ1 = Σ2 up to integer multiples of π. This arithmetic angle relation is a certificate obstructing equidecomposability/equicomplementability when impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application: using Bricard's condition to rule out equidecomposability
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute dihedral angles for given polyhedra; if the required integer linear relation between angle sets (mod π) cannot hold (e.g., would force a rationality that contradicts known irrationality), then the polyhedra are not equidecomposable/equicomplementable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: regular tetrahedron dihedral angle α = arccos(1/3) and cube angles π/2 imply impossibility; other tetrahedra (orthogonal-edge tetrahedron, orthoscheme) yield angles arccos(1/√3), π/6, π/2 etc., and irrationality results (from Chapter 7) are used to conclude non-equidecomposability with cubes or other tetrahedra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: convex polytope and convex hull representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A convex polytope in R^d is the convex hull of a finite set S = {s1,...,s_n}, i.e., P = conv(S) = {Σ λ_i s_i : λ_i ≥ 0, Σ λ_i = 1}. Equivalently, a convex polytope is the bounded solution set of a finite system of linear inequalities P = {x ∈ R^d : A x ≤ b}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both vertex (convex-hull) and halfspace (inequality) representations are used interchangeably. Facets correspond to supporting hyperplanes; these representations underpin many combinatorial and geometric arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: face of a polytope
rubrics_metrics.description: A face F of P is a subset of the form P ∩ {x ∈ R^d : a^T x = b} where a^T x ≤ b is a valid inequality for all x ∈ P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faces are themselves polytopes; 0-faces are vertices, (d−1)-faces are facets. The facet hyperplane HF determines two closed halfspaces, one of which contains P — a fact used later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph of a convex polytope and Euler's formula context
rubrics_metrics.description: The graph G(P) of a convex polytope has vertex set V (the vertices of P) and edge set E (1-dimensional faces). For 3-dimensional polytopes this graph is planar and Euler's polyhedron formula applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combinatorial graph viewpoint is used to connect polytope geometry with planar graph theorems in later chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruence vs combinatorial equivalence of polytopes
rubrics_metrics.description: Two polytopes P and P' are congruent if a length-preserving affine map (possibly orientation-reversing) maps P to P'. They are combinatorially equivalent if there is a bijection between their faces preserving dimension and inclusion relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinatorial equivalence is weaker than congruence: polytopes can share the same face-lattice (same 'combinatorial type') while having different metric geometry (e.g., a skew cube vs unit cube).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: centrally symmetric polytope
rubrics_metrics.description: A set P ⊆ R^d is centrally symmetric if there exists x0 ∈ R^d with x0 + x ∈ P ⇔ x0 − x ∈ P for all x. The point x0 is called the center of P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard symmetry notion used in classifying polytopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sylvester–Gallai theorem (two-point line existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any configuration of n points in the real plane, not all on a single line, there exists a line that contains exactly two of the points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kelly's proof uses a minimal-distance argument (choose point and line minimizing distance), relying on metric and order axioms of the real plane. The Fano plane shows that incidence axioms alone are insufficient; some further order/metric property is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős–de Bruijn theorem (number of lines ≥ n)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a set P of n ≥ 3 points in the plane not all collinear, the set L of lines passing through at least two points contains at least n lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction using Sylvester–Gallai: remove one point on a 2-point line and apply the induction hypothesis to the remainder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motzkin/Conway incidence theorem (m ≥ n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be a set of n ≥ 3 elements and A1,...,Am proper subsets such that every pair of elements of X is contained in precisely one Ai. Then m ≥ n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short proofs include a counting/inequality argument attributed to Motzkin/Conway and a linear-algebra proof using the incidence matrix B and the fact that B B^T is positive definite so rank(B) ≥ n, hence m ≥ n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph decomposition results (cliques and bipartite decompositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decomposing the complete graph K_n into cliques (each edge in exactly one clique) requires at least n cliques. Decomposing K_n into complete bipartite subgraphs requires at least n−1 such subgraphs (Graham–Pollak theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bipartite decomposition lower bound has no known purely combinatorial proof and is typically proved via linear algebraic arguments (e.g., Tverberg's proof). The obvious decomposition into stars uses n−1 bipartite graphs, showing tightness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic graph-theory definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of graphs G = (V,E), simple graphs (no loops/multiedges), adjacency (neighbors), incidence (vertex-edge), subgraph, induced subgraph, connectedness, path, clique, independent set, forest, tree, bipartite graph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These standard notions are recalled to support the combinatorial theorems and decompositions discussed; see the appendix for illustrations and further terminology.
